name: sort, then only neighbours can clash
hook: Do any two of {n} meetings clash? You don't compare {pairs} pairs. You sort, and compare {neighbours} neighbours.
hook_sub: Sort by start, and overlap becomes a question about neighbours.
caption: Can one person attend every meeting? Only if no two overlap, and a meeting that ends exactly when the next begins is fine.
Comparing every pair of {n} meetings is {pairs} comparisons when nothing clashes. Sort by start first, and you compare each meeting only with the one before it: {neighbours} comparisons.

Why that is enough: say meeting j overlaps some earlier meeting i. The meeting right before j starts no earlier than i and no later than j, so i is still running when it starts too. Push that down and some adjacent pair must clash. So if no neighbours clash, nothing does.
One detail: the comparison is <, not <=. With <=, [[1,5],[5,8]] is wrongly rejected.
Where else does sorting turn an all-pairs question into a neighbour question? 👇
cta: Next in the module: Insert Interval.

slides.h: Can one person attend them all?
p: Only if no two meetings overlap. One ending exactly when another begins is fine.

slides.h: Sort, and it's a neighbour question
p: Sort by start. If two meetings anywhere in the list overlap, then two *adjacent* meetings must overlap.
So one pass decides it: compare each meeting's start against the previous meeting's end. That end is the only state you carry.
`<`, not `<=`: with `<=`, `[[1,5],[5,8]]` would be wrongly rejected.
Say meeting *j* overlaps some earlier meeting *i*.
The meeting right before *j* starts no earlier than *i* and no later than *j*. So *i* is still running when it starts too.
Push that down and some adjacent pair must clash. If no adjacent pair clashes, no pair does.
The sort costs O(n log n). The scan after it carries one value.
